title: Services are expanding global trade while connectivity, payments, skills, and rule-making capacity leave least developed countries behind
source_unit: UN Trade and Development, Global Trade Update (September 2026): Services are reshaping global trade, but least developed countries lag in digital exports
geography: Global services trade, developed and developing economies, and least developed countries

observations.period: 2022-2025; services embedded in production and global exports

denominator.unit: global trade and intermediate-input percentage reference

services_intermediate_inputs.unit: percent of global intermediate inputs accounted for by services in 2022

services_global_exports.unit: percent of global exports represented by services in 2025

services_export_growth.unit: percent growth in global services exports in 2025

production_route.value: services increasingly underpin manufacturing, agriculture, and participation in global value chains

observations.method: UN Trade and Development synthesis of trade statistics, intermediate-input data, services exports, and value-chain participation.
observations.uncertainty: Aggregate services shares do not show local value capture, wages, job quality, bargaining power, tax incidence, or whether growth reaches households and smaller firms.
observations.subgroup: Services firms, manufacturers, agricultural producers, digital-platform and logistics providers, workers, consumers, and economies diversifying into services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Services growth can create new entry points for firms and workers, but it can also increase dependence on concentrated platforms, infrastructure, and standards.

observations.period: 2015-2025; digitally deliverable services and country-group divergence

digital_services_growth.unit: percent average annual growth in digitally deliverable services over the past decade

digital_services_global_share.unit: percent of global services exports represented by digitally deliverable services

ldc_services_export_share.unit: percent of global services exports accounted for by least developed countries in 2025

ldc_digital_export_share.unit: percent of least developed countries’ services exports that are digitally deliverable

observations.method: UN Trade and Development comparison of global and country-group services exports and digitally deliverable services.
observations.uncertainty: Country-group shares hide substantial variation among least developed countries and do not measure domestic employment, profitability, inclusion, or the quality and affordability of connectivity.
observations.subgroup: Least developed countries, developing-country exporters, digital-service workers, firms, governments, and consumers dependent on cross-border digital access.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low current participation can leave room for rapid catch-up where infrastructure, skills, finance, regulatory capacity, and market access improve; digital exports are not the only development pathway.

observations.period: 2025-2026; infrastructure, payment, skill, and AI-readiness constraints

denominator.unit: UNCTAD structural assessment of digital-services trade participation

participation_constraints.value: connectivity gaps, costly international payments, and skills shortages constrain participation in digitally deliverable services

ai_strategy_adoption.value: less than one third of developing countries have adopted national AI strategies

concentration_risk.value: computing capacity, data, finance, and expertise remain concentrated in a small number of economies and firms

policy_route.value: digital infrastructure, skills, payment systems, and AI readiness are joint conditions for inclusive services trade

observations.method: UN Trade and Development synthesis of digital-trade participation barriers, payment costs, skills, computing concentration, and national AI-policy readiness.
observations.uncertainty: The update identifies structural constraints but does not estimate the causal contribution of each barrier, the cost of closing gaps, or which policy mix will generate durable local capabilities.
observations.subgroup: Digital-service exporters, small firms, workers and learners, payment providers, network operators, regulators, and countries with limited computing and financing capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentrated infrastructure and expertise can lower entry costs or improve reliability in some settings, while targeted partnerships may transfer capability if governance and bargaining power are credible.

observations.period: 2000-2025; digital trade rules and participation in rule-making

pta_digital_provisions_2000_2025.unit: percent of preferential trade agreements signed between 2000 and 2025 containing e-commerce or digital-trade provisions

developed_country_recent_participation.unit: percent of developed countries participating since 2020 in agreements containing digital-trade provisions

developing_country_recent_participation.unit: percent of developing countries participating since 2020 in agreements containing digital-trade provisions

ldc_recent_participation.unit: percent of least developed countries participating since 2020 in agreements containing digital-trade provisions

governance_route.value: fragmented digital-trade rules can make transparency, regulatory cooperation, and negotiating capacity consequential for who benefits

observations.method: UN Trade and Development inventory and comparison of preferential trade agreements and digital-trade provisions since 2000 and 2020.
observations.uncertainty: Agreement participation does not establish implementation, market access, enforcement, firm use, consumer benefit, or meaningful negotiating influence for any country.
observations.subgroup: Trade negotiators, regulators, developing and least developed countries, digital firms, workers, and consumers subject to emerging digital rules.
observations.counterinterpretation: New digital provisions can improve predictability and access when capacity-building and interoperability accompany them; rule fragmentation may sometimes reflect legitimate local policy choices.

related_sources.claim: Earlier UNCTAD trade update provides complementary geopolitics, value-chain, food-security, and regulation context.
UNCTAD digital-economy work provides complementary data, infrastructure, and development context.

boundary: This record adds a services-trade route from digital growth through connectivity, payment, skills, AI capacity, and fragmented rule-making. It is aggregate publication evidence, not firm-level causal analysis, worker outcomes, household welfare, infrastructure quality measurement, or proof that digital trade produces inclusive development.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official UNCTAD September 2026 Global Trade Update page was reviewed for services shares and growth, least developed country participation, digital constraints, AI strategy adoption, and digital-trade agreement patterns.
